title: Child Labor: Not Funny
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of child labor in the United States and the world. They start with the Puritan work ethic and colonial farm labor, contrast it with medieval England, and move through the Industrial Revolution, the Gilded Age robber barons, and jobs kids held (cotton mill bobbin changing, canneries, breaker boys in coal mines, tenement piecework like cigar rolling, newsboys). They cover the 1899 newsboys strike, the National Child Labor Committee and photographer Lewis Hine, the slow legislative fight from the 1906 Beveridge proposal through the 1916 Keating-Owen Act and the Great Depression, and the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act with its minimum wage and youth work limits. They end with current child labor worldwide (about 158 million victims, tobacco and mercury mining), the ILO's four recommendations, and the International Year for the Elimination of Child Labor. A listener mail closes the episode.
topics: International Year for the Elimination of Child Labor

segments.title: Opening and framing child labor
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, written by Josh's daughter at Dave Ruse's suggestion, and compare their own teenage paper routes and first jobs with real child labor. They note the International Year for the Elimination of Child Labor.
topics: International Year for the Elimination of Child Labor

segments.title: Colonial work ethic and childhood in medieval England
segments.summary: The hosts describe how colonial American children, especially farm children, started working around age thirteen, citing the Puritan work ethic. They contrast this with medieval England, where children played until puberty.

segments.title: Industrial Revolution and early factory child labor
segments.summary: Alexander Hamilton's view that women and children were made more useful by manufacturing is cited. Josiah Quincy's account of a cotton spinning factory with four-year-old workers is described, along with photographs of beaten-down child workers.

segments.title: Second Industrial Revolution and robber barons
segments.summary: The hosts explain how steel, coal, and railroads expanded demand for child and immigrant labor during the Gilded Age. They describe the robber barons' exploitation of workers with little oversight.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments with off-topic banter.

segments.title: Jobs held by children: canneries, mills, coal, tenements
segments.summary: The hosts describe jobs kids held: canning and shucking in canneries, bobbin changing in textile mills, breaker boys in Pennsylvania coal, and tenement piecework such as cigar rolling and paper flowers. Josh shares a personal story about a family envelope-stuffing job and a delivery route.

segments.title: Newsboys strike and nicotine poisoning
segments.summary: The hosts describe newsboys buying papers wholesale and selling them, and the 1899 newsboys strike that won buybacks of unsold papers. They then discuss nicotine poisoning from handling tobacco, including child tobacco workers in Zimbabwe, and Josh recounts smoking as a kid.

segments.title: Progressive movement and National Child Labor Committee
segments.summary: The hosts discuss progressive reformers who pushed for school-first rules and limits on child work, including Jane Addams, Julia Lathrop, Lillian Wald, and Francis Perkins. They describe the National Child Labor Committee, formed in 1904, and its photographer Lewis Hine, who documented child workers in disguise.

segments.title: Legislation history and Fair Labor Standards Act
segments.summary: The hosts trace the failed and partial attempts at child labor law, from the 1906 Beveridge proposal to the 1916 Keating-Owen Act struck down by the Supreme Court. The Great Depression opened the way for the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act, which set the first federal minimum wage of 25 cents and the under-16 manufacturing and mining limits. They also discuss the later minimum wage increases and the current federal minimum of $7.25.

segments.title: Current US child labor rules and agricultural exemptions
segments.summary: The hosts summarize current federal rules, including hazardous work limits, the three-hour school-day limit under sixteen, the under-fourteen restriction, and the exemption for homemade evergreen wreath making. They note that agricultural child labor has far fewer protections, including for children working on family farms.

segments.title: Global child labor and ILO solutions
segments.summary: The hosts describe child labor worldwide, with an estimated 158 million victims, including gold mining with mercury and tobacco farms. They list the ILO's recommendations: expanding education, helping families meet basic needs through income support and microloans like Kiva, improving adult wages and supply chain oversight, and funding enforcement. Germany's new supply chain law is mentioned, and CODE is praised for its education work.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ellie
segments.summary: A listener from Louisville, Kentucky, writes about using the podcast in long-term care with cognitive impairment clients and praises the show, including the snake handling episode. Josh and Chuck also correct a Kentucky location mix-up.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and sign off, with the show credited to iHeartRadio.
